Palos Heights has 4,762 housing units and a median build year of 1976. 58.1 percent of them were built before 1980, 35.9 percent before 1970 and 2.5 percent before 1940. Those three numbers together describe the walls, the trim and the windows better than a photograph does.

Owner households here number 4,280 and renter households 215, a 95.2 percent owner-occupied place. The stock behind those households is 60.8 percent detached, 22.6 percent attached and 16.5 percent multi-unit, at a median of 6.5 rooms. The Census puts the median home value at $350,000.

Palos Heights is in the top four of the 54 suburbs and towns covered here for the highest owner-occupied share (95.2 percent) and the largest townhome and rowhouse share (22.6 percent).

Compared with the 76 place average behind this site, Palos Heights is unusual for townhomes and rowhouses at 22.6 percent against a 7.5 percent average, prewar housing at 2.5 percent against a 15.8 percent average and housing in buildings of two or more at 16.5 percent against a 29 percent average.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2019-2023 (tables B25003, B25024, B25034, B25035, B25077). Every dollar figure on this page is a published Census estimate of what homes in the area are worth. None of it is a price for work.

How the age of the stock changes the work here

The garage is half the exterior on a lot of 1976 plans and it is routinely left off the quote. Overhead door, jamb, the trim above it and the service door add up to a real piece of work on the 60.8 percent of Palos Heights that is detached houses. Ask whether it is in or out before you compare two numbers. 22.6 percent of the housing here is attached, so a fair share of the work is townhome and association work: matching an existing scheme exactly, working to a board's schedule and painting several identical units in a row.

What an estimate here has to account for

  • Matching, exactly. 22.6 percent of units are attached, and on a shared elevation close is not good enough. Existing color has to be matched rather than approximated.
  • Finish level. With a median home value of $350,000, the finish standard people expect here is higher than the standard a fast quote is priced at. Worth agreeing before rather than after.
  • Distance, stated. Palos Heights is 5.3 straight-line miles from the shop. Travel to Palos Heights is not a hidden line item on this site and it should not be one on a written quote either.
  • Containment, not just paint. 58.1 percent of housing in Palos Heights was built before 1980, so on most addresses here the lead-safe setup and the cleanup are part of the job and part of the hours.

Most of it is 1970s stock with a large share of townhomes and apartment units. Association work, matching an existing scheme exactly and painting several identical units in a row, is as much of the Palos Heights market as single-house work.

What the age of the housing here means for an interior job

58.1 percent of housing units were built before 1980, the nearest bucket to the 1978 line that the Census publishes, and that is the reading for Palos Heights. Housing that old falls under the federal Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, which covers any work disturbing paint in a home built before 1978. Illinois is not an authorized state for it, so EPA runs it here directly.

The practical content of it is dust. Where paint in a Palos Heights room gets disturbed past about six square feet, twenty outside, or wherever a window comes out, the work has to be contained and cleaned to a standard. That is time at both ends of the job, and it is why an honest quote on 4,280 homes worth of 1976-median housing reads longer than a fast one.

None of it is graded at the town line. The rule attaches to a build year and to the work being done, so the number worth checking is the one on your own deed in Palos Heights.

The useful question is not whether the rule applies to your Palos Heights house. At 35.9 percent pre-1970 it very likely does. The useful question is what the containment and the cleanup are actually going to look like in your rooms, and it is a fair one to ask anybody.

From the shop

Palos Heights is among the most owner-occupied places on this list, about 95 percent, with only a couple of hundred renter households in the whole city. There is effectively no turnover or landlord market here. What there is instead is repeat homeowner work on 1970s houses that have generally been kept up: repaints on a cycle, trim and door replacement, and exterior wood that has been maintained rather than left. That is a different job from a neglected exterior and it should be priced as one, in both directions.

Questions

Asked about Palos Heights

Who actually shows up in Palos Heights?

Mike Walsh owns the company, walks the job and stays on it while our crew works. Call 708-935-4289. It is worth saying because on a job this size the gap between whoever measured it and whoever turns up is where most of the disappointment comes from.

Can it be done a room at a time?

Yes. With a median of 6.5 rooms in Palos Heights a full interior is a real commitment, and there is nothing wrong with taking it in pieces. The one thing worth planning is the order, so that the rooms that get used most are not the ones sitting under plastic in December.

What changes the price most on a house here?

The state of the trim and the ceilings. Wall area is predictable, and with 6.5 median rooms and a 1976 median build year in Palos Heights the woodwork is where the hours actually go. Ask for it as its own line and the differences between two quotes stop being mysterious.

Most of Palos Heights is owner occupied. Does that change anything?

It changes what the work usually is. At 95.2 percent owner occupied, with 4,280 owner households, there is very little turnover painting here and a lot of repeat maintenance: exteriors on a cycle, one room at a time inside, trim and doors when they finally go. A maintained house and a neglected one are different jobs and should be different numbers, in both directions.
